lines: Every second, a company network carries thousands of connections.
Almost all of them are normal. A tiny few are attacks.
This is NetSentinel, my solution for DataNova problem DN-CY-01: a system that finds those few, including attacks it has never seen before.
Think of airport security: thousands of ordinary passengers, and only now and then someone dangerous.
In the real traffic I used, the rarest attack is one connection in forty-five thousand.
A lazy guard who waves everyone through is right almost all the time, and completely useless.
A model trained the naive way becomes that lazy guard: it looks accurate, and catches nothing.
So NetSentinel has to solve four problems at once.
Attacks are rare, so training is rebalanced: the model sees rare attacks more often.
New attacks appear, so a second detector learns only what normal traffic looks like, and flags anything unfamiliar.
Tactics change, so a drift monitor watches the traffic and asks for retraining.
And analysts drown in alerts, so alerts become explained incidents, and every analyst decision teaches the model.
Here is how it works.
Network flow records come in, one row per connection, and are cleaned and checked for leaks.
Two detectors look at every flow: a rebalanced ensemble for known attacks, and a novelty detector for the unknown.
Their alerts become incidents, each with a priority, a reason, and a first response.
The analyst confirms or rejects them, and the model retrains on those decisions. One command runs the whole loop.
To prove it on real traffic, I used CIC-IDS2017 from the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity.
Five working days of a real network: 2.8 million flows, with attacks staged on different days.
Nine attack families, and forty-five thousand to one between the biggest and the smallest.
The raw files are messy, so the pipeline repairs them automatically: a twelve-hour clock with no A M or P M, almost three hundred thousand empty rows, and three hundred thousand duplicates.
On 121 thousand test flows the system had never seen,
99.9 percent of attack flows raise an alert,
and only one normal flow in a thousand raises a false alarm.
Macro F1, which weights every attack family equally, rises from 0.77 to 0.97 with rebalancing.
But to be honest: most of that jump comes from just nine flows of the two rarest families. On the others, the gain is small, but statistically real.
Now the most important result.
Shuffle the data randomly, and the score is 0.97.
Keep each attack session on one side, and it drops to 0.89.
Train on the past and test on the future, and it collapses to 0.18.
Every attack in this dataset happens on a single day, so a model trained on Monday to Thursday has never seen Friday's attacks. A supervised detector only knows yesterday's attacks.
That is why NetSentinel has a second detector.
It learns only what normal traffic looks like, and flags flows that look like nothing it knows.
To test it, I hide one attack family from training at a time.
Web attacks go from 3 to 87 percent caught, denial of service from 3 to 71 percent, and on average from 5 to 33 percent, for about one percent more false alarms.
Port scans and botnets still look normal at flow level. That is a real limit, and I report it.
Attackers also change tactics over time.
Trained on the first days, the model scores 0.998 on them, but only 0.18 on the days that follow.
The drift monitor notices this without any labels: the alerted traffic shifts, and unknown anomalies rise from 0.9 to 5.4 percent.
After retraining on just ten percent of the new flows, the score recovers to 0.93.
Detection is only useful if a person can act on it.
On the test traffic, the models raised 22,601 flow alerts.
The console groups them into 483 incidents, by attack family, shared endpoint and time: forty-seven times fewer things to open.
Here it scores five thousand new flows: 952 alerts become 60 incidents, fourteen of them top priority.
Opening an incident shows why it was raised: the features furthest from normal traffic.
It shows how sure the model is, as a set of possible families with a ninety percent guarantee for each family.
It suggests a first response.
And one analyst decision labels the whole incident, so the model can retrain on it.
Every number in this project can be checked.
Each headline result has a confidence interval.
The same model is tested three ways: random, by session, and over time.
An automatic audit looks for shortcuts and leaks before training, and eighty-one automated tests guard the code.
NetSentinel has clear limits.
Port scans and botnets look normal at flow level, the novelty detector costs about one percent extra false alarms, and the data is from 2017.
Next, I would pair it with payload inspection such as Zeek or Suricata, tune the alert budget to the size of the team, and run it on the official DataNova data with a single command.
NetSentinel finds rare attacks, flags new ones, and keeps analysts in the loop, with honest numbers on real traffic.
The code, the report and this video are on GitHub. Thank you.
